title: A Whole City Turns Around
overview: Jonah finally delivers God's warning to Nineveh, the whole city from ordinary people up to the king responds with grief and change, and God holds back the disaster.

parts.label: Jonah's second chance (vv. 1-3a)
parts.note: After running away and being swallowed by the great fish in the earlier chapters, Jonah hears almost the same command again. This time he simply goes.

parts.label: An enormous city (v. 3b)
parts.note: Nineveh was a major city of Assyria, the empire that later conquered northern Israel, so it was enemy territory for Jonah's people. Scholars are unsure what "three days" means: the time to walk across it, the size of the wider district, or the time needed to cover it while preaching.

parts.label: A very short warning (v. 4)
parts.note: In Hebrew Jonah's message is only five words, with no call to change and no offer of mercy. The word for "overthrown" can also mean "turned around," and many readers see a quiet hint of how things will end.

parts.label: The people respond (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Fasting, wearing sackcloth (rough cloth like sacking) and sitting in dust or ashes were common ways to show grief and humility. The response starts with ordinary people and reaches all the way to the king, who sets aside his royal robe.

parts.label: The king's order (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: Even the animals are made to fast and wear sackcloth, which matches ancient customs of including livestock in public mourning. The king calls for real change, especially an end to violence, yet openly admits no one can be sure God will spare them.

parts.label: God holds back (v. 10)
parts.note: Seeing them turn from their evil ways, God does not bring the destruction that was announced, which many read as showing the warning was conditional all along. Christians later noted that Jesus held up Nineveh's turning as an example to the people of his own day.

disagreement: Christians differ on what it means that God changed course and held back the announced disaster: some take it as God truly responding to people, while others hold that God does not change and the threat was always meant to be conditional.
think: When someone you see as an enemy seems to genuinely change, what makes it hard or easy to accept that they might not get what they once deserved?
